name: Pedro Moreau

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for meeting me, Pedro. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or political parties. This is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Weekdays I'm on a big site out by the motorway, building a distribution warehouse for one of the online shops. I'm a junior carpenter with the fit-out contractor, so I put up the office partitions inside, the timber decking on the mezzanine floors, fire doors, that sort of thing. My supervisor, Craig, still checks my door frames because I'm not quick or neat enough yet. It's a huge shed, you could fit ten football pitches in it.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: What I really like is the weekends. I build decks and fences for people round my area, I find the jobs on local ads, and I use AI every day to price them, draw them and write the quotes. That's how I'm saving for my own van. What wears me out is the weekday site, it's all the same and you're one of two hundred people in hi-vis, and I live with my older brother Luis, who thinks I work too much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fine, it's a good tool, I use it every day and it makes me money. I'd probably post a video of me quoting a deck in five minutes with it, just to show people. Nobody needs to be scared of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's actually perfect. I get to use it to grow my weekend business, and nobody else is using it to replace me. I'd be my own boss in five years, I reckon.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep the warehouse job for steady money and keep the weekends going. I've got about three months saved, and I'd put the rest towards the van this year. Then maybe in two years I go full time on my own, decks, fences, garden rooms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, good. Like the coast is clear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why keep the weekday job if the weekend work is what you love?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'm not stupid with money. My dad lost his little café when I was fifteen, he went all in and had nothing to fall back on. So I keep the wage until the side business pays the bills on its own for six months straight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Luis say about the plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He says I'll burn out before thirty. He's probably half right. But he also borrowed my AI quoting thing for his plastering work last week, so he can't talk.

S0.say: I'd say it's a good tool that I use every day and it makes me money. I'd post a video of quoting a deck in five minutes so people see there's nothing to fear.
S0.think: Privately it's perfect for him: he uses AI to grow his weekend business and nobody uses it to replace him. He expects to be his own boss in five years.
S0.do: Keeps the warehouse job for steady pay and builds decks and fences at weekends. Puts money beyond his three months of savings towards a van this year and plans to go full time on his own in about two years.
S0.feel: Calm and good, like the coast is clear.
S0.quote: So I keep the wage until the side business pays the bills on its own for six months straight.
S0.fieldNote: Pedro is an energetic side-hustler who already uses AI to win weekend work. His caution comes from watching his father lose a café with nothing to fall back on. He sees technology as a way to become his own boss.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a good time to be quick and willing. The people who learn it do well, the ones who complain get left behind. I'd say that online, and probably get a few angry replies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think it's great for me. I'm already ahead with the tools, and if quoting and design get even easier I can do more jobs for less effort. The weekday site might shrink, but I wasn't planning to stay anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy the van this year and go fully on my own sooner, maybe in a year instead of two. I'd look at a small cutting machine or whatever new kit comes out to speed up decks. And I'd keep three months saved, no less, because of my dad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, excited really. This is my kind of picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the people who complain get left behind. Would you feel any sympathy for them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, of course. Some of the older guys on the warehouse site, like Craig, they've done it thirty years one way. I'd help them if they asked, I just don't think the government should pay people to sit at home instead of learning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could go wrong for you in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bigger firms using the same tools to offer decks cheaper than me. Then it's a price war, and I'm one guy with a van. I'd have to compete on being local and turning up when I say I will.

S1.say: I'd say it's a good time to be quick and willing: those who learn do well and those who complain get left behind. I'd say it online and expect some angry replies.
S1.think: Privately he thinks it's great for him, since he's already ahead with the tools and quoting and design get easier. The warehouse site might shrink, but he wasn't planning to stay.
S1.do: Buys the van this year and goes fully self-employed within a year instead of two. Buys new kit such as a small cutting machine for decks while keeping at least three months saved.
S1.feel: Calm and excited, as this is his kind of picture.
S1.quote: Then it's a price war, and I'm one guy with a van.
S1.fieldNote: Steady change speeds up Pedro's plans to go solo. His sympathy for older workers is real but bounded by his dislike of paying people not to work. He names bigger firms with the same tools as his real risk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is going to hit everyone, so be smart and move fast. I'd still say people should work and not wait for handouts, but I'd be less cocky about it. It's not the same as just learning a new app.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, two years is scary even for me. If a robot can build a deck and the AI can do the quote and the sale, then what am I? A guy with a van and a laptop, doing what the robot does, only slower.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can. Keep in mind there are only about 2 years before it arrives.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't buy the van, I'd keep the cash and build my savings to six months. I'd try to get a job with whoever's selling or fitting the building robots, because for a year or two they'll need people who know sites. And I'd talk to Luis about combining our money, maybe buying one robot between us if they get cheap enough to hire out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Restless, I'd want to do ten things at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd buy a robot with Luis. Is that realistic with your savings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not straight away, no. Three months of savings doesn't buy a robot. But maybe a used one, or a share of one with a few other tradesmen, like how farmers share a combine harvester.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your dad say about this plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd tell me not to go all in, like he did with the café. He'd say keep the cash under the bed. Honestly, in this picture, he might be right for once.

S2.say: I'd say it will hit everyone, so be smart and move fast. I'd still say people should work rather than wait for handouts, but I'd be less cocky about it.
S2.think: Privately two years scares even him: if robots build decks and AI does the quote and sale, he's just a slower version of the robot with a van and a laptop.
S2.do: Drops the van purchase and builds savings to six months. Seeks a job with a firm selling or fitting building robots, and explores pooling money with his brother or other tradesmen to share a robot.
S2.feel: Anxious and restless, wanting to do ten things at once.
S2.quote: A guy with a van and a laptop, doing what the robot does, only slower.
S2.fieldNote: The fast picture deflates his confidence and he admits he'd be less cocky. He reaches for ownership again, but with realistic limits, borrowing the image of farmers sharing a combine harvester. His father's warning about going all in suddenly sounds right to him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a real chance for anyone willing to work. Learn the machines, start something, don't sit around. That's what I'd tell my cousins and anyone online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think five years is enough for me to get on the right side of it. I'd have my own business with a van by year one or two, and by year four I'd want a robot or two working for me instead of me competing with them. I'd be thirty-two and owning kit, not being replaced by it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can. This time there are about 5 years of warning.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go self-employed next year, as planned, and use the money from decks to save for robots. I'd do short courses on running and maintaining building robots, the ones the makers run. Around year three I'd try leasing a robot and pricing jobs that use it, so I learn the business before everyone else does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. There's a flicker of nerves, but it's the good kind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens when everyone else has the same idea?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then it comes down to who's quicker and who customers trust. I'd want to be the guy in town people already know from the decks. Being first matters, and I'm usually first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where does your faith or family come in, if at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mum would make sure I'm at Mass on Sunday whatever I'm doing. Honestly, family's my safety net, not the government. If it all goes wrong, Luis and I would look after each other, like we always have.

S3.say: I'd say five years is a real chance for anyone willing to work: learn the machines, start something, don't sit around. I'd tell my cousins and people online.
S3.think: Privately he thinks five years is enough to get on the right side of it: his own business soon, then robots working for him by year four. At thirty-two he'd own kit rather than be replaced by it.
S3.do: Goes self-employed next year and saves decking profits for robots. Takes maker-run courses on running building robots and tries leasing one around year three to learn the business early.
S3.feel: Mostly calm, with a flicker of good nerves.
S3.quote: Being first matters, and I'm usually first.
S3.fieldNote: With five years, Pedro sees himself as an owner of machines rather than a competitor to them. His plan is staged and money-aware, with leasing before buying. Family, not government, is his stated safety net, and his mother keeps faith in the picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, there's no excuse for anyone. Start a business, learn a trade, learn the machines. I'd be saying that loudly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years is ideal for me. I'd have a proper business by thirty, a couple of lads working for me, and by the time AGI lands I'd own the robots. At thirty-seven I'd want to be the boss of a small firm, not on anyone's payroll.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can. This time there are about 10 years of warning.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, buy the van, go on my own, build a name with decks and garden rooms. Around year four or five, start bringing in robots for the heavy work and train my own lads to run them. Keep at least six months of the business's costs in the bank by then, because of what happened to Dad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, even excited. This is the one I'd pick.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Some people say ten years makes people lazy. Would it make you lazy?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No chance. If anything I'd go faster, because I'd know the window. The ones who'll be lazy are the ones waiting for someone to tell them what to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would worry you, if anything, in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Giant companies owning all the robots and renting them out at whatever price they like. Then a guy like me can't compete. I'd want rules that keep the market open, not handouts, just a fair shot for small firms.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is plenty and there's no excuse for anyone: start a business, learn a trade, learn the machines. I'd say it loudly.
S4.think: Privately ten years is ideal: a business by thirty, a couple of workers, and owning robots when AGI arrives. At thirty-seven he wants to be the boss of a small firm.
S4.do: Buys the van and goes self-employed in the first year, building a name with decks and garden rooms. Brings in robots for heavy work around year four or five, trains his workers to run them and keeps six months of business costs in the bank.
S4.feel: Calm and excited; it's the picture he'd choose.
S4.quote: If anything I'd go faster, because I'd know the window.
S4.fieldNote: The long horizon fits Pedro's entrepreneurial plan exactly. His one worry is concentration: giant firms owning all the robots and setting rental prices. He wants open markets and fair rules for small firms, not handouts, which fits his traditional outlook.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because there's no time to build anything, and three months of savings doesn't buy you a robot. What would help is small loans for tradesmen to buy or share machines, and rules that stop a few giant companies owning all of them.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask what people like me are good at that robots aren't. I turn up, I shake your hand, I remember your dog's name. I don't know if that's worth anything in 2036, but I'm betting it is.

headlineQuote: I turn up, I shake your hand, I remember your dog's name. I don't know if that's worth anything in 2036, but I'm betting it is.
portrait: Pedro Moreau is a 27-year-old junior carpenter fitting out a huge distribution warehouse on weekdays, who builds decks and fences at weekends and uses AI every day to price and win the work. He lives with his older brother Luis, has about three months saved and is putting money towards a van, cautious because his father lost a café. He is calm and even excited in the first two pictures, which speed up his plan to go solo. AGI in two years makes him anxious and humbler, while five or ten years make him calm again, planning to own robots rather than compete with them.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because there's no time to build anything and his savings won't buy a robot.
whatWouldHelp: Small loans for tradespeople to buy or share machines, and rules that stop a few giant companies owning all the robots.
